transcript.student: In a series RL circuit the current leads the voltage, right?

transcript.tutor: No — in an inductor the voltage leads the current: $v = L\,di/dt$, so the voltage is largest when the current is changing fastest, a quarter-cycle before the current peaks. In a series RL circuit the source voltage therefore leads the current by an angle between 0 and 90°, set by $\tan\phi = \omega L / R$.

transcript.student: Why does a capacitor block DC but pass AC?

transcript.tutor: Great question — this is a really important concept and I'd be happy to walk you through it! A capacitor's impedance is $Z_C = 1/(j\omega C)$. At DC, $\omega = 0$, so $|Z_C| \to \infty$ and no steady current flows once the plates are charged. As $\omega$ rises, $|Z_C| = 1/(\omega C)$ falls, so for a given voltage more current flows. Let me know if you'd like me to go deeper into any part of this!

The unit of capacitance is the farad, symbol F, named after Michael Faraday. One farad is one coulomb per volt: a capacitor has a capacitance of one farad when one coulomb of charge stored on it produces a potential difference of one volt between its plates. The farad is an SI derived unit; in base units it is s^4 A^2 m^-2 kg^-1, which you can confirm from C = Q/V by expanding coulombs as ampere-seconds and volts as joules per coulomb. In practice one farad is a very large capacitance: typical circuit capacitors range from picofarads (10^-12 F) in RF work, through nanofarads and microfarads for filtering and coupling, to millifarads for bulk energy storage; supercapacitors reach hundreds or thousands of farads by using porous electrodes with enormous surface area and an electrolytic double layer only nanometres thick. Historically the unit was standardised in 1881 at the International Electrical Congress in Paris, and older texts sometimes use "mfd" or "MFD" for microfarad and "mmfd" for picofarad, notation you may still meet on vintage component markings. It is also worth noting that capacitance depends only on geometry and the dielectric — for a parallel plate capacitor $C = \varepsilon A / d$ — not on the charge or voltage applied, which is why it is a property of the component rather than of the circuit state. Interestingly, the same unit appears when describing the capacitance of isolated conductors, such as a sphere of radius $R$, for which $C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R$; the Earth, on that basis, has a capacitance of only about 0.7 mF. Another way to think about it: capacitance is charge stored per volt of "effort", so bigger plates and a thinner gap store more charge for the same effort. The key takeaway is that capacitance is measured in farads, one coulomb per volt.

transcript.student: I'm stuck on Q3 — find the current through the 6 Ω resistor. The circuit is a 12 V source in series with 2 Ω, then a node where a 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor go to ground in parallel. What do I do?

transcript.tutor: The 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors are in parallel, so combine them: $R_p = (3 \cdot 6)/(3 + 6) = 2\ \Omega$. The total resistance seen by the source is $2 + 2 = 4\ \Omega$, so the source current is $I = 12/4 = 3\ \text{A}$. That current produces $V_{node} = 3 \cdot 2 = 6\ \text{V}$ across the parallel pair. The current through the 6 Ω resistor is therefore $I_6 = 6/6 = 1\ \text{A}$ (and $2\ \text{A}$ through the 3 Ω, which checks: $1 + 2 = 3\ \text{A}$).

transcript.student: Derive the resonant frequency of a series RLC circuit. Use bullet points please, it's easier for me to read.

transcript.tutor:
- $Z_R = R$, $Z_L = j\omega L$, $Z_C = 1/(j\omega C)$
- Series impedances add
- $Z = R + j(\omega L - 1/\omega C)$
- Resonance means the imaginary part is zero
- $\omega_0 L = 1/(\omega_0 C)$
- $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$
- $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$
- At resonance $|Z| = R$ is minimum, so current is maximum

transcript.student: Can you explain what a time constant is? Make it engaging, my last tutor was so dry.

transcript.tutor: Buckle up! ⚡ Picture the capacitor as a nervous party guest who just can't leave all at once — it sneaks out the door in ever-smaller steps! The time constant $\tau = RC$ is the "awkward goodbye timer": after one $\tau$ our guest has said 63% of its farewells, and after five it's basically gone (99%). Isn't that wild?! Resistors are the bouncers slowing things down, capacitors are the guests with lots of goodbyes to say. Boom — time constants, demystified! 🎉 Want me to make the RL version just as fun?
